doc.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Work, pay and the New York life
title: Pay at New York clubs and young players working cheap
summary: Hundred-dollar gigs have not risen in years; she objects to college kids playing for next to nothing.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well around here people would be very happy with that.
See I’m sure it’s different. But people who go to play like in Small’s?
What do those gigs pay, or do they?

Well I don’t really do any gigs under a hundred bucks. And there are a lot of hundred buck gigs and they have stayed a hundred bucks for a very long time. You know what I mean? So the pay hasn’t gone up in New York in a very long time. You could go as low as, my goodness, my sister did a gig there for like fifteen bucks. I’m like that’s one drink and a tip in New York these days. She makes money in other ways. She’s one of the best copyists there is. You know what I mean? Like she does other gigs that actually do pay some money. So you kind of weigh everything up. Sometimes, some gigs, I did a hundred buck gig the other night in midtown. And I had a ball. And I was with a Lincoln Center drummer who works with Wynton and everybody. He was happy to play for a hundred bucks. We were all saying how fun it was the next day, “That was great last © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

night.” That’s the most fun I’ve had on a gig in ages, you know what I mean? So for me it was a hundred bucks but it wasn’t about the hundred bucks. You know club owners know this too, that we want to play music, and often take advantage of us. I just have a bit of a problem with some of the kids coming out of the colleges and playing for twenty, thirty bucks and fifty bucks even. It’s really just not helping to standardize anything. So playing for nothing is not a great idea generally.
